newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian government may seek '97 budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Russian government may seek '97 budget cuts.

text.p: The Russian government is likely to try to cut 1997 budget spending this month because tax revenues are well behind schedule, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Monday.

Deputy Finance Minister Sergei Shatalov said that spending cuts -- known as sequestering -- would be in line with the 1997 budget law, which says the government has to cut spending if revenues fall below 90 percent of quarterly budget targets.
"It looks as though the government will submit a proposal on sequestration of spending as early as April," Shatalov told a news conference. He said official revenue plans were unrealistic.

The International Monetary Fund has already delayed paying several tranches of its $10 billion three-year loan to Russia because of low tax receipts and government officials admit low revenue is a major problem.
A massive publicity campaign has tried to encourage Russians to pay their taxes, but revenues remain stubbornly low.
Deputy Prime Minister Alfred Kokh said at the weekend that tax collection in the first quarter was only 58 percent of that budgeted for. He called it "a crisis of statehood".
Shatalov said March tax revenues could be as low as 19 trillion roubles, well below the 21.9 trillion forecast by the state tax inspectorate last month.
"This budget needs to be much more realistic. We need to cut down our spending significantly," he said.

Alexander Pochinok, a member of the budget committee of the State Duma lower house of parliament, told the news conference revenue shortfall for the year could reach as much as 100 trillion roubles -- amounting to almost a quarter of proposed 1997 revenue of 433 trillion roubles.
But he said a special law would be needed for the government to sequester spending.

"It's clear that we need a special law on sequestration - that's the tragedy. I mean we need to cut deep, including even protected items," said Pochinok, calling for the government to submit a draft law this month.

The Russian budget lists several key "protected items" where spending cannot be cut. But spending plans have been ignored in the past, and the IMF last year criticised the government for not meeting its spending promises.
